title: Fit meta-analysis models
text:
Now we’ll fit multilevel meta-analytic models in the R package metafor (Viechtbauer 2010). This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/2_analysis/2 fit meta analysis models.R that includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.
Given the non-independence structures in this data we will fit a series of models with increasingly complex random effects, particularly to control for phylogenetic similarity between prey species and to also deal with non-phylogenetic components of species identity. We’ll create a model guide to organize these models, as well as our subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses. These analyses include:
Note that instead of including habitat type, locomotion, or landform as categorical predictors, we used separate univariate (intercept-only) models on these subgroups of the data. In part this is to keep the code cleaner (the results are the same regardless) but also because in most cases there was only one factor level of these variables with sufficient data to estimate coefficients and we were not interested in testing for differences between factor levels.

title: Fit meta-analysis models
text:
Prepare the dataset
Let’s reload our dataset. We’ll clean up the article ID to be a bit friendlier as a text string in the models and we’ll add a variable to our dataset to specify whether the effect size type was dominant (for filtering out minority converted effect sizes). Finally, we’ll reshape our dataset to be long by our habitat and landform variables to make our models easier to succinctly fit:

Code# Load prepared data:
dat <- fread("builds/meta_analysis/analysis_ready_dataset.csv")

# Clean up the article ID a bit:
dat[, article_id := paste(word(Article, 1, 
                               sep = "[[:space:][:punct:]]"), 
                          .GRP), 
    by = .(Article)]

# Check that that didn't screw anything up:
length(unique(dat$Article)) == length(unique(dat$article_id))

nrow(dat[duplicated(article_id)]) == nrow(dat[duplicated(Article)])
# Must be TRUE

# >>> Add column for whether effect size type is dominant within analysis group --------
dat[, total_n_articles := uniqueN(article_id), by = .(analysis_group)]
dat[, n_articles_per_original_es := uniqueN(article_id), by = .(analysis_group,
                                                                     original_effect_size)]
dat[, dominant_effect_size := ifelse((n_articles_per_original_es / total_n_articles) > .5,
                                          "yes", "no")]
dat[, .(n = .N), by = .(dominant_effect_size)]

# >>> Make data long by habitat traits ------------------------------------
# Instead of having these as separate factors, let's do univariate subgroup models
dat.long <- melt(dat,
                 measure.vars = c("locomotion_volant",
                                  "ground_or_burrow_resting_or_nesting",
                                  "Foraging_habitat_ground", "continent_island"),
                 variable.name = "habitat_category",
                 value.name = "habitat_trait")

dat[, habitat_trait := "All"]
dat[, habitat_category := "All"]

dat.final <- rbind(dat[, !c("locomotion_volant",
                            "ground_or_burrow_resting_or_nesting",
                            "Foraging_habitat_ground", "continent_island"),
                       with = F], 
                   dat.long)
head(dat.final)

# Now let's format these names and concatenate with variable type.
unique(dat.final[, .(habitat_category, habitat_trait)])
dat.final[habitat_trait != "All", 
          habitat_trait := paste0(habitat_category, ".", 
                                  habitat_trait)]


The variable habitat_trait will allow for easy subgroup filtering as we fit our models.

title: Fit meta-analysis models
text:
Set up model guide
Now let’s create all the combinations of models we want to run. The function data.table::CJ is similar to expand.grid and makes all combinations of the input vectors. We’ll do this in two steps to avoid having to filter out some combinations that we don’t have sample size to run.

Code# # Do the guide in 2 steps. We don't have enough data for class * habitat sub-analyses.
guide <- CJ(analysis_group = unique(dat.final$analysis_group),
            moderator = c("1", "log_mass"),
            class = c("Birds", "Mammals", "Reptiles", "All"),
            habitat_trait = "All",
            prey_range = c("All", "inside"),
            non_phylo_species = c("yes", "no"),
            phylo_species = c("yes", "no"),
            only_dominant_effect_size = c("yes", "no")
)
guide <- guide[!(moderator == "log_mass" & class != "All"), ]

guide2 <- CJ(analysis_group = unique(dat.final$analysis_group),
             moderator = "1",
             habitat_trait = c("locomotion_volant.non_volant", 
                               "locomotion_volant.volant", 
                               "ground_or_burrow_resting_or_nesting.other",
                               "ground_or_burrow_resting_or_nesting.ground", 
                               "Foraging_habitat_ground.other",
                               "Foraging_habitat_ground.ground", 
                               "continent_island.island", 
                               "continent_island.mainland"),
             class = c("All"),
             prey_range = c("All"),
             non_phylo_species = c("yes", "no"),
             phylo_species = c("yes", "no"),
             only_dominant_effect_size = c("no")
             )

guide <- rbind(guide, guide2)


Now we’ll add a unique ID that we’ll use to compare alternative random effects per model series (model_comparison_id). And we’ll formulate strings which we’ll evaluate as R code for our random effects (random_effect), to filter our dataset (exclusion) and for our fixed effect formula (formula):

Codeguide[, model_comparison_id := paste0("model_comp_", .GRP), 
      by = .(analysis_group, class, moderator, prey_range,
             habitat_trait, only_dominant_effect_size)]

guide[, random_effect := "list(~1|article_id/Effect_size_ID"]

guide[, random_effect := ifelse(non_phylo_species == "yes",
                                paste0(random_effect, ", ~1|scientificName"), 
                                paste0(random_effect))]
guide[, random_effect := ifelse(phylo_species == "yes",
                                paste0(random_effect, ", ~1|phylo_species)"),
                                paste0(random_effect, ")"))]
guide

# Formulate exclusion formula:
guide[, exclusion := paste0("analysis_group == '", analysis_group, "'",
                            " & habitat_trait == '", habitat_trait, "'")]
guide[class != "All", exclusion := paste0(exclusion, " & class %in% '", class, "'")]

guide[prey_range == "inside", 
      exclusion := paste0(exclusion, " & prey_range_primary == 'inside'")]
guide[prey_range == "All"]

#
guide.m1 <- merge(guide,
               unique(dat[, .(analysis_group, analysis_effect_size)]),
               by = 'analysis_group',
               all.x = T)
guide.m1[is.na(analysis_effect_size)]
guide.m1

#
guide.m1[only_dominant_effect_size == "yes", 
         exclusion := paste0(exclusion, " & dominant_effect_size == 'yes'")]

#
guide.m1[, formula := ifelse(moderator == "1",
                             "~ 1",
                             paste("~", moderator))]


guide.m1[, model_id := paste0("model_", seq(1:.N))]

The columns exclusion, random_effect, and formula are text strings that we will evaluate to filter the dataset and run models.
Now we’ll filter out models for which we have insufficient sample size. We’ll do this by evaluating the exclusion strings as a subsetting operation on the dataset. We’ll be very generous with sample size inclusion criteria and will fit models if there are at least 2 observations for intercept-only models and 5 observations for models with a continuous moderator (body mass).

CodeNs <- list()
sub.dat <- c()

for(i in 1:nrow(guide.m1)){
  sub.dat <- dat.final[eval(parse(text = guide.m1[i, ]$exclusion)), ] # Evaluate `esclusion` string
  
  Ns[[i]] <- sub.dat[, .(n_species = uniqueN(scientificName),
                    n_articles = uniqueN(Article),
                    n_obs = .N,
                    model_id = guide[i, ]$model_id,
                    analysis_group = guide[i, ]$analysis_group,
                    class = guide[i, ]$class)]
  Ns[[i]]$model_id <- guide.m1[i, ]$model_id
  
}
Ns <- rbindlist(Ns)

guide.m2 <- merge(guide.m1, 
               Ns[, .(n_species, n_articles, n_obs, model_id)], 
               by = "model_id")

title: Publication bias tests
text:
Given that some of our analysis contain mixed effect sizes we elected to only conduct time-lag publication bias tests. Other publication bias tests (e.g., small sample size) require uniform measurements of effective sample size or variance and are not suitable for original effect size types.
Time lag publication bias tests asks if significant effects have declined (or increased) since initial discovery, which is common when strong initial findings spur the development of a field. We thus regress our effect sizes against publication year. We’ll do a similar approach with a model guide as we did above. Except we’ll put all of the code into a single code block. This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/2_analysis/4 publication bias.R that includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.

Code# Clean environment:
rm(list = ls())

# Load packages
library("data.table")
library("metafor")
library("ggplot2")
library("ggstance")
library("orchaRd")
library("patchwork")
library("readxl")
library("stringr")
library("sf")
library("mapview")
library("dplyr")
library("rotl")
library("broom.mixed")
library("here")

rma_predictions <- function(m, 
                            newgrid,
                            has_intercept = T){
  
  
  if(!is.data.frame(newgrid)){errorCondition("ERROR newgrid must be a data frame")}
  #create the new model matrix. 
  
  if(!all(unlist(lapply(names(newgrid), # lapply through names of newgrid to check that they're in formula
                        function(x) grepl(pattern=x,
                                          x = as.character(m$formula.mods)[-1]))))){
    errorCondition("ERROR: variables in newgrid are not in model formula")
  }
  
  
  # Drop levels that might be missing from the model...
  cols <- names(newgrid)
  coef_nms <- names(coef(m))
  temp <- c()
  
  if(has_intercept == F){
    
    for(i in 1:length(cols)){
      if(class(unlist(newgrid[, cols[i], with = F])) %in% c("factor", "character")){
        temp <- paste0(names(newgrid[, cols[i], with = F]),
                       unlist(newgrid[, cols[i], with = F]))
        newgrid <- newgrid[temp %in% coef_nms, ]
      }
    }
    
  }
  
  newgrid
  
  # Create prediction matrix
  predgrid <- (model.matrix(m$formula.mods, data=newgrid))
  predgrid
  
  if(any(grepl("intercept", colnames(predgrid), 
               ignore.case = TRUE))){
    #if intercept is present, remove it?
    predgrid <- predgrid[, -1]
  }
  
  # predict onto the new model matrix
  pred.out <- as.data.frame(predict(m, newmods=predgrid))
  
  #attach predictions to variables for plotting
  final.pred <- cbind(newgrid, pred.out)
  
  return(final.pred)
}


# Load data ---------------------------------------------------------------

dat <- fread("builds/meta_analysis/analysis_ready_dataset.csv")

dat[, article_id := paste(word(Article, 1, sep = "[[:space:][:punct:]]"), .GRP), by = .(Article)]

nrow(dat[duplicated(article_id)])
nrow(dat[duplicated(Article)])
# Must be equal. Good

dat.long <- copy(dat)

# >>> Extract publicaiton years ------------------------------------------
library("readr")

# parse_number(x = "Gerber, G.P. and Iverson, J.B., 2000. Turks and Caicos iguana, Cyclura carinata carinata. West Indian Iguanas: Status Survey and Conservation Action Plan. IUCN the World Conservation Union, Gland, Switzerland, pp.15-18.")

            "\\d+")

dat.long[, year := str_extract(Article,
                               "\\d+")]
unique(dat.long$year)
dat.long[year == "6", ]$Article

dat.long[, year := as.numeric(year)]

# Because of mixed effect size types, let's just do time-lag publication bias?

dat.long[, year_scaled := scale(year)]

# Set up model guide -----------------------------------------------------------------

unique(dat.long$analysis_group)


guide <- CJ(analysis_group = unique(dat.long$analysis_group),
            moderator = c("year_scaled")
)

guide[, random_effect := "list(~1|article_id/Effect_size_ID"]

guide[, exclusion := paste0("analysis_group == '", analysis_group, "'")]
# guide[class != "All", exclusion := paste(exclusion, "& class == '", class, "'")]

guide[, formula := paste("~", moderator)]

guide

guide[, model_id := paste(analysis_group, moderator)]

# Run models --------------------------------------------------------------

bias_models <- list()
bias_tidy <- list()
i <- 1

for(i in 1:nrow(guide)){
  sub.dat <- dat.long[eval(parse(text = guide$exclusion[i]))]
  
  bias_models[[i]] <- try({
                            rma.mv(yi_analysis,
                             V = vi_analysis,
                             method = "REML",
                             test = "t",
                             dfs = "contain",
                             mods = as.formula(guide$formula[i]),
                             random = ~1 | article_id/Effect_size_ID,
                             data = sub.dat)
  })
  if(!inherits(bias_models[[i]], "try-error")){
    bias_tidy[[i]] <- bias_models[[i]] |> 
      tidy() |>
      mutate(sigma = min(bias_models[[i]]$sigma2),
             df = paste(bias_models[[i]]$ddf, collapse = ", "),
             lower_ci = bias_models[[i]]$ci.lb,
             upper_ci = bias_models[[i]]$ci.ub) |>
      bind_cols(guide[i, ]) |>
      setDT()
  }

  
}

bias_models

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
We converted the effect sizes into common types based on the formulas in (Borenstein et al. 2021), which we digitized in our function convert_effect_sizes. The formulas are in an executable sidecar csv file located at scripts/functions/conversion_formulas.csv
Codesource("scripts/functions/convert_effect_sizes.R")

formulas <- fread("scripts/functions/conversion_formulas.csv")
We’ll show the formulas below, demonstrate the use of the function, and the digitized R formulas.

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
SMD → lnOR
Let \(yi_{lnOR}\) and \(yi_{d}\) be the point estimate for the lnOR and Cohen’s d effect sizes and \(vi_{lnOR}\) and \(vi_{d}\) be their sampling variances. The resulting estimate of Cohen’s d was then converted using Equation 3 to Hedges’ g.
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_{lnOR} = yi_d * \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} \\
&vi_{lnOR} = vi_d * \frac{\pi^2}{3} \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]
In R:

Codeconvert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "lnOR",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes that the continuous data has a logistic distribution. 
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with `metafor::escalc` package defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g') 


   yi_trans   vi_trans
      <num>      <num>
1: 1.677835 0.03289868


Now let’s look at the transcribed formula for the point estimate conversion. yi and vi refer to the original effect size and sampling variance estimates (in this case of lnOR) and yi_trans and vi_trans refer to the converted estimates (in this case of SMD), n1 and n2 = \(n_{1, 2}\), and d = \(yi_d\). Note that our formula for \(J\) uses the gamma distribution instead of \(J = 1 - \frac{3}{4 * (n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1}\):


J <- ifelse((n1 + n2 - 2) <= 1, NA_real_, exp(lgamma((n1 + n2 - 2)/2) - log(sqrt((n1 + n2 - 2)/2)) - lgamma(((n1 + n2 - 2) - 1)/2)))
d <- yi / J
yi_trans <- d * (pi / sqrt(3))


And for sampling variance:


vi_trans <- vi * (pi^2/3)

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
lnOR → SMD
To convert from lnOR (\(yi_{lnOR}\)) to Cohen’s \(d\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_d = yi_{lnOR} * \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\
&vi_d = vi_{lnOR} * \frac{3}{\pi^2} \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]
\(yi_d\) was then converted to Hedges’ g using Equation 3.
In R:

Codeconvert_effect_sizes(from = "lnOR",
                     to = "SMD",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes that the response variable is a discretized version of a continuous variable 
with a logistic distribution for each group (which approximates the normal distribution).
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses with and without converted data. 


   yi_trans    vi_trans
      <num>       <num>
1: 0.482765 0.003039636


And the transcribed formulas in R:


d <- yi * (sqrt(3)/pi)
J <- ifelse((n1+n2-2) <= 1, NA_real_, exp(lgamma((n1+n2-2)/2) - log(sqrt((n1+n2-2)/2)) - lgamma(((n1+n2-2) - 1)/2)))
yi_trans <- J * d


And for sampling variance:


vi_trans <- vi * (3/pi^2)


The variable names are the same as above.

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
SMD → Zr
To convert from SMD to Zr, we used Equation 2 to convert Hedges’ g to Cohen’s d. We then converted \(yi_d\) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and then to Zr, using a correction factor \(a\), to account for cases where \(n_1 \neq n_2\). Let \(yi_{Zr}\) and \(yi_d\) be the point estimate for Zr and Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&a = \frac{(n_1 + n_2)^2}{n_1*n_2} \\
&r = \frac{yi_d}{\sqrt{yi_d^2 + a}} \\
&r \leftarrow \min(1, \max(-1, r_i))\\
&yi_{Zr} = atanh(r)\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]
And the sampling variance of Zr (\(vi_{Zr}\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&n = n1 + n2 \\
&vi_{Zr} = \frac{1}{(n - 3)} \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]
In R:

Codeconvert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "Zr",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes a continuous variable was dichotomized to create the treatment and control groups. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with 'metafor::escalc' defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g'). 
Like usual, be careful :) 


    yi_trans   vi_trans
       <num>      <num>
1: 0.4474395 0.03703704


And let’s look at the R formulas. yi and vi refer to the original effect size and sampling variance estimates (in this case of SMD) and yi_trans and vi_trans refer to the converted estimates (in this case of Zr), n1 and n2 = \(n_{1, 2}\), a = the correction factor \(a\), and d = \(yi_d\). Note that our formula for \(J\) uses the gamma distribution instead of \(J = 1 - \frac{3}{4 * (n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1}\):


J <- ifelse((n1 + n2 - 2) <= 1, NA_real_, exp(lgamma((n1 + n2 - 2)/2) - log(sqrt((n1 + n2 - 2)/2)) - lgamma(((n1 + n2 - 2) - 1)/2)))
d <- yi / J
a <- (n1 + n2)^2 / (n1 * n2)
r <- d/sqrt(d^2 + a)
yi_trans <- atanh(r)


And for sampling variance:


N <- n1 + n2
vi_trans <- 1 / (N-3)

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
Zr → SMD
First, convert the point estimate of Zr (\(yi_{Zr}\)) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and calculate the variance of \(r\) (\(vi_r\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&r = tanh(yi_{Zr}) \\
&vi_r = \frac{(1-r^2)^2}{(n-1)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\]
Then calculate the point estimate (\(yi_d\)) and variance (\(vi_d\)) of Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_d = \frac{2*r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \\
&vi_d = \frac{4*vi_r}{(1-r^2)^3} \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}\]
Cohen’s d (\(yi_d\)) was then converted to Hedges’ g following Equation 3.
In R:

Codeconvert_effect_sizes(from = "Zr",
                     to = "SMD",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n = 50)

'yi' is assumed to be 'Zr' (r-to-z transformed correlation coefficient). 
It may be preferable to supply 'r' and 'n' instead. To do so specify 'r' in the 'from' argument and provide a vector of correlation coefficients named 'r'. 
This conversion assumes that the underlying data was continuous with a bivariate normal distribution, with the two groups created by dichotomozing one of the two variables. 
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses 


   yi_trans vi_trans
      <num>    <num>
1: 2.037275 0.167652


And here are the transcribed formulas used:


r <- tanh(yi)
d <- (2*r) / sqrt(1-r^2)
J <- ifelse((2*n - 2) <= 1, NA_real_, exp(lgamma((2*n - 2)/2) - log(sqrt((2*n - 2)/2)) - lgamma(((2*n - 2) - 1)/2)))
yi_trans <- d * J


And for sampling variance:


r <- tanh(yi)
vi_r <- (1 - r^2)^2 / (n-1)
vi_trans <- (4*vi_r) / (1-r^2)^3


The variable names are the same as above.

title: Citation network
text:
In this page we will plot and analyze the citation network uncovered by following all claimant and non-claimant sources regarding the effects of cats on threatened wildlife.
Claimant sources are reviews that claimed that cats were a driver of endangerment and are treated separately than non-claimants, which included a systematic search in Web of Science along with opportunistic records found and a published systematic review (Wallach and Lundgren 2025).
This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/2_analysis/1 citation networks and bias.R that includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.

title: Prepare meta-analysis dataset
text:
Now we’ll meta-analyze the quantitative articles that provided data usable for a meta-analysis. We’ll start by calculating effect sizes and then converting effect sizes to a common type for analysis based on our analysis groups. This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/1_data_mgt/5 clean meta-analysis that includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.
We’ll then run a suite of models and choose the model with the best random effects. Finally, we’ll plot the resulting model estimates and conduct publication bias tests.

title: Prepare meta-analysis dataset
text:
Prepare environment
We’ll start by loading packages and some helper functions. The convert_effect_sizes function contains formulas to convert between effect sizes. The formulas were originally provided by Borenstein et al. (2021). The get_r function is a simple helper function for extracting the correlation coefficient (r) from the cor.test output.

Coderm(list = ls())

library("data.table")
library("metafor")
library("readxl")
library("stringr")
library("sf")
library("mapview")
library("dplyr")

source("scripts/functions/convert_effect_sizes.R") # This function converts between effect sizes

get_r <- function(x, y){
  out <- cor.test(x, y)
  return(out$estimate)
}

title: Prepare meta-analysis dataset
text:
Calculate effect sizes
We’ll start by loading the raw extracted data. Given the heterogeneity in experimental designs, the raw data was collected in 3 separate spreadsheets based on the data structure required for each effect size type. We’ll load these into a list object:

Codefiles <- c("data/meta_analysis/Cat meta-analysis - SMDs.xlsx",
           "data/meta_analysis/Cat meta-analysis ORs.xlsx",
           "data/meta_analysis/Cat meta-analysis - correlations.xlsx")
dat_list <- lapply(files, read_excel)
names(dat_list) <- c("SMDs", "ORs", "Zrs")


We also have a separate file that gives analysis groups for each effect size—e.g., how to group effect sizes for each model. These groupings are also the scaffold for some of our sensitivity analyses (e.g., different degrees of lumping across different experimental treatment types).
The analysis groups include:

Abundance with/without cats
Abundance before-after eradication
Abundance on islands with/without cats
Abundance spatial association
Abundance temporal association
Reproduction with/without cats
Reproduction before-after eradication
Reproduction temporal association

The ‘with/without cats’ is a broader analysis group that includes the data in ‘before-after eradication’ and ‘islands with/without cats’.

Codeanalysis_groups <- read_excel("data/meta_analysis/analysis groups.xlsx",
                              skip = 0) |> setDT()

unique(analysis_groups[, .(Description, final_analysis_group1, final_analysis_group2)])

z-to-r-transformed correlation coefficients (Zr) effect sizes
We’ll start with the correlation coefficient (Zr) effect sizes.
Note that several effect sizes in this dataset can be analyzed either as Zr effect sizes (with binary predictor) or SMD. We’ve decided that they would best be analyzed as SMD effect sizes, which we handle in the code below.
Because the variance of proportion data increases closer to 0/1 boundaries, we stabilized variance with arc-sin square root transformation and the delta method following Macartney et al. (2022).

Codecor <- dat_list[["Zrs"]] |> setDT()

sort(unique(cor$Effect_size_ID))

# >>> Clean -------------------------------------------------------------------
unique(cor$Description)

cor[Description == "Spatial correlation" & Effect_size_ID == "ES_3", ]

# Make variables numeric:
cor[is.na(as.numeric(Prey_correlation_data))]$Prey_correlation_data

cor[is.na(as.numeric(Prey_correlation_data))]$Prey_correlation_data

cor.sum <- cor[!is.na(Cat_correlation_data), 
               .(r = get_r(x = Cat_correlation_data,
                           y = Prey_correlation_data),
                   n = .N),
               by = .(Effect_size_ID, scientificName,  Description,
                      unit_of_replication,
                      Article, Article_secondary_same_data, 
                      analysis_group, effect_size_type, Abundance_reproduction,
                      Prey_units, Cat_units, Source, Analysis_comment, 
                      Latitude, Longitude, Study_location)]

cor.sum[duplicated(Effect_size_ID)]
cor.sum[Effect_size_ID == "ES_32", 
        Effect_size_ID := paste0(Effect_size_ID, "_", .GRP), 
        by = .(scientificName)]

cor.sum <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
                     ri = r, ni = n,
                     data = cor.sum) |> setDT()

length(unique(cor.sum$Effect_size_ID))
length(unique(cor.sum$Article))

cor.sum[, original_effect_size := "Zr"]

# Final Zr dataset:
cor.final <- copy(cor.sum)


Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) effect sizes
Now let’s calculate SMD for the effect sizes in the SMD file. This data reflects two discrete treatments (cats present, cats absent) with a continuous response variable summarized as mean±SD.

Codesmd <- dat_list[["SMDs"]] |> setDT()
head(smd)

# >>> Clean -------------------------------------------------------------------
# setnames(smd, "...30", "analysis_group_notes")
smd[is.na(as.numeric(Prey_mean_cats_Absent))]
smd[is.na(as.numeric(Prey_mean_cats_Present))]
smd[is.na(as.numeric(Prey_error_cats_Absent))]
smd[is.na(as.numeric(Prey_error_cats_Present))]
smd[is.na(as.numeric(Sample_size_overall_cats_Absent))]
smd[is.na(as.numeric(Sample_size_overall_cats_Present))]
smd[, `:=` (Prey_mean_cats_Absent = as.numeric(Prey_mean_cats_Absent),
            Prey_mean_cats_Present = as.numeric(Prey_mean_cats_Present),
            Prey_error_cats_Absent = as.numeric(Prey_error_cats_Absent),
            Prey_error_cats_Present = as.numeric(Prey_error_cats_Present),
            Sample_size_overall_cats_Absent = as.numeric(Sample_size_overall_cats_Absent),
            Sample_size_overall_cats_Present = as.numeric(Sample_size_overall_cats_Present))]

unique(smd$Effect_size_ID)


# >>> Drop N < 3 ----------------------------------------------------------
smd <- smd[Sample_size_overall_cats_Absent >= 3 &
             Sample_size_overall_cats_Present >= 3, ]


# >>> Calculate effect sizes --------------------------------------------------
setnames(smd, c("Sample_size_overall_cats_Absent", "Sample_size_overall_cats_Present"),
                c("n2", "n1")) # This is to prevent later confusion while converting

smd <- escalc(measure = "SMD",
              m2i = Prey_mean_cats_Absent, m1i = Prey_mean_cats_Present,
              sd2i = Prey_error_cats_Absent, sd1i = Prey_error_cats_Present,
              n2i = n2, n1i = n1,
              data = smd) |> setDT()
smd[, .(Prey_mean_cats_Absent, Prey_mean_cats_Present, yi)]

smd[, original_effect_size := "SMD"]

# smd <- rbind(smd)
smd$analysis_group

# smd[converted_to == "Zr"]
smd.final <- copy(smd)


log Odds Ratio (lnOR) effect sizes
Now we’ll calculate our odds ratio effect. This data has two discrete predictors (cats present / absent) and a binary outcome variable (present versus absent or nest fledged versus failed).

Codeor <- dat_list[["ORs"]] |> setDT()
or

#
or <- escalc(measure = "OR",
             ai = Prey_and_cat_positive,
             bi = Prey_negative_cat_positive,
             ci = Prey_positive_cat_negative,
             di = Prey_and_cat_negative,
             data = or) |> setDT()
or

or[, n1 := Prey_and_cat_positive + Prey_negative_cat_positive]
or[, n2 := Prey_positive_cat_negative + Prey_and_cat_negative]
or[, original_effect_size := "lnOR"]
or.final <- copy(or)


Bind effect size datasets together and prepare analysis groups
Now we bind these datasets together:

Codemeta_combined <- rbind(cor.final, smd.final, or.final, fill = T)

# Make sure there are no duplicated effect sizes
meta_combined[duplicated(Effect_size_ID)]

Empty data.table (0 rows and 39 cols): Effect_size_ID,scientificName,Description,unit_of_replication,Article,Article_secondary_same_data...


Now we’re going to merge in the analysis groups, for which there are multiple effect size ID. This merge will increase the number of rows of the dataset (but each effect size will only be in each model once because the analysis group variable will be unique for each model).

Codemeta_combined[, key := paste(Abundance_reproduction, Description)]
analysis_groups[, key := paste(Abundance_reproduction, Description)]

analysis_groups <- melt(analysis_groups,
                        id.vars = c("key"),
                        measure.vars = c("final_analysis_group1", "final_analysis_group2"),
                        variable.name = "analysis_group_level",
                        value.name = "final_analysis_group")
analysis_groups <- analysis_groups[!is.na(final_analysis_group)]
analysis_groups[, analysis_group_level := ifelse(analysis_group_level=="final_analysis_group1",
                                                 "fine_scale", "lumped")]

setdiff(meta_combined$key, analysis_groups$key)
setdiff(analysis_groups$key, meta_combined$key)

analysis_groups[, .(n = uniqueN(final_analysis_group)), by = .(key)]
# 

meta_combined.mrg <- merge(meta_combined[, !c("analysis_group")],
                           unique(analysis_groups[, .(key, analysis_group_level, final_analysis_group)]),
                           by = "key",
                           allow.cartesian = TRUE,
                           all.x = T)

meta_combined.mrg[is.na(final_analysis_group)]

meta_combined.mrg[, n_effect_types := uniqueN(original_effect_size),
                  by = .(final_analysis_group)]
meta_combined.mrg[n_effect_types == 1, ]

setnames(meta_combined.mrg, "final_analysis_group", "analysis_group")


Let’s check that the units of replication are not too different per analysis group:

Codemeta_combined.mrg[, .(n_units = uniqueN(unit_of_replication),
                      units = paste(unique(unit_of_replication), collapse = "; ")),
                  by = .(analysis_group)]

                            analysis_group n_units                   units
                                    <char>   <int>                  <char>
 1:     Abundance before-after eradication       2          Plots; Surveys
 2:            Abundance with/without cats       3 Plots; Surveys; Islands
 3:     Abundance inside/outside exclosure       1                   Plots
 4: Abundance on islands with/without cats       1                 Islands
 5:          Abundance spatial association       2            Plots; Sites
 6:                  Abundance correlation       2            Plots; Sites
 7:         Abundance temporal association       1                   Plots
 8:  Reproduction before-after eradication       2          Nests; Surveys
 9:         Reproduction with/without cats       2          Nests; Surveys
10:  Reproduction inside/outside exclosure       1                   Nests
11:       Reproduction spatial association       1                   Sites
12:               Reproduction correlation       2            Sites; Nests
13:      Reproduction temporal association       1                   Nests


We think that these are close enough to be acceptable given the limited data available.

title: Prepare meta-analysis dataset
text:
Convert effect sizes
Now we’ll begin to convert effect sizes. We’ll start by splitting out analysis groups that are a single effect size type (i.e., don’t require conversion).

Codeone_type <- meta_combined.mrg[n_effect_types == 1, ]

one_type[n_effect_types == 1, `:=` (yi_analysis = yi,
                                    vi_analysis = vi,
                                    analysis_effect_size = original_effect_size)]
nrow(one_type)

[1] 77

Codelength(unique(one_type$analysis_group))

[1] 9


Now we’ll deal with mixed groups. First we’ll determine what the dominant group is and use this to designate the analysis effect size for each analysis group.

Codemixed_types <- meta_combined.mrg[n_effect_types > 1, ]

# Determine dominant effect size type per analysis group
mixed_types[, .(paste(sort(unique(original_effect_size)), 
                      collapse = "; ")),
                by = .(analysis_group)]

type_freq <- mixed_types[, .(n = .N),
                 by = .(analysis_group, original_effect_size)]
setorder(type_freq, analysis_group)

type_freq <- type_freq[, .SD[which.max(n)], by = .(analysis_group)]

setnames(type_freq, "original_effect_size", "analysis_effect_size")

mixed_types <- merge(mixed_types,
                     type_freq[, .(analysis_group, analysis_effect_size)], 
                     by = "analysis_group",
                     all.x = T)

mixed_types[analysis_group %in% c( "Reproduction spatial association"),
            analysis_effect_size := "SMD"]

mixed_types[is.na(analysis_effect_size), ]

already_converted <- mixed_types[analysis_effect_size == original_effect_size, ]
to_convert <- mixed_types[analysis_effect_size != original_effect_size, ]

#
to_convert[, key := paste(original_effect_size, analysis_effect_size)]


We’ll now loop over this dataset based on the unique combinations of original effect size (original_effect_size) and destination effect size (analysis_effect_size). The effect size formulas we use here are given here.

Codecombos <- unique(to_convert$key)
combos
out <- list()

convert_effect_sizes(formula_path = "scripts/functions/conversion_formulas.csv")

for(i in 1:length(combos)){
  sub_dat <- to_convert[key == combos[i]]
  
  out[[i]] <- convert_effect_sizes(n = n, 
                                   n1 = n1, n2 = n2,
                                   yi = yi, vi = vi, 
                                   r = r,
                                   from = unique(sub_dat$original_effect_size),
                                   to = unique(sub_dat$analysis_effect_size),
                                   data = sub_dat,
                                   bind = TRUE,
                                   formula_path = "scripts/functions/conversion_formulas.csv")
}

converted <- rbindlist(out)
setnames(converted, c("yi_trans", "vi_trans"), c("yi_analysis", "vi_analysis"))
already_converted[, `:=` (yi_analysis = yi, vi_analysis = vi)]


Now we’ll bind the dataset back together:

Codemixed_type <- rbind(converted, already_converted)
mixed_type[is.na(yi_analysis), ]

Empty data.table (0 rows and 45 cols): analysis_group,key,Effect_size_ID,scientificName,Description,unit_of_replication...

Codemeta.final <- rbind(one_type, mixed_type)

text:
Merge in covariates
Body mass
Now we’ll merge in covariates. We’ll start with body mass. Body mass for mammals was derived from PHYLACINE [Faurby2018-wu] and is available for download here. Body mass for birds was derived from Avonet (Tobias et al. 2022) and is available for download here. Body mass for reptiles and species absent from the other datasets include (San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Library 2015; IUCN 2018; Gibbs et al. 2001).

Codespecies <- data.table(scientificName = unique(c(meta.final$scientificName)))

species[, spp_name_corrected := scientificName]
species[scientificName == "Pampusana erythroptera", 
        spp_name_corrected := "Gallicolumba erythroptera"]

# Mammals:
phyl <- fread("data/trait_databases/phylacine_traits.csv")

phyl[, Binomial.1.2 := gsub("_", " ", Binomial.1.2)]

species.m1 <- merge(species, phyl[, .(Binomial.1.2, Order.1.2, 
                                      Mass.g)],
                    by.x = "spp_name_corrected", by.y = "Binomial.1.2",
                    all.x = T, all.y = F)

# Birds:
avonet <- read_excel("data/trait_databases/AVONET Supplementary dataset 1.xlsx",
                     "AVONET1_BirdLife") |> setDT()
unique(avonet$Species1)

species.m1[scientificName %in% avonet$Species1]

species.m2 <- merge(species.m1,
                    avonet[, .(Species1, Order1, Mass)],
                    by.x = "spp_name_corrected", by.y = "Species1",
                    all.x = T, all.y = F)

species.m2

species.m2[, Mass_g_final := ifelse(is.na(Mass.g), Mass, Mass.g)]
species.m2[, Order_final := ifelse(is.na(Order.1.2), Order1, Order.1.2)]
species.m2[is.na(Mass_g_final)]

species.m2[, source := fcase(!is.na(Order.1.2), "Phylacine 1.2",
                             !is.na(Order1), "Avonet",

species.m2[, class := fcase(!is.na(Order.1.2), "Mammals",
                             !is.na(Order1), "Birds",
                             is.na(Order.1.2) & is.na(Order1), NA)]


species.m2[is.na(Mass_g_final)]
species.m2[spp_name_corrected == "Chelonoidis niger", `:=` (Order_final = "Testudines",
                                                            Mass_g_final = 80,# weight at birth

                                                           Mass_g_final = 113.5,

species.m2[is.na(class), ]

meta.final.mrg

title: Systematic review
text:
This section will tally the evidence types encountered. This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/2_analysis/3 meta and review summary.R, which includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.
Prepare environment & load data:

Plot evidence types found
Now we’ll do some quality control checks, clean up factor levels, create color palettes and plot this.

Codesys_rev <- sys_rev[exclude_species == "included_species",]
n_studies <- sys_rev[, .(n_studies = uniqueN(study_id)),
                     by = .(evidence_type, has_data, of_quality, Hypothesis_supported,

              `Population in support without data` = "dodgerblue4", 
              `Population in support with data` = "dodgerblue",
              `Population in support with data and qualities` = "dodgerblue"
              )

n_studies$synth_fill <- factor(n_studies$synth_fill,
levels = (c("Predation not in support", 
            "Predation in support", 
            "Population not in support without data",
            "Population not in support with data",

            "Population in support without data",

            )))

                                     grepl("Population", evidence_type), "Population")]

                    y = abs(n_studies), fill = synth_fill, color = of_quality))+
  geom_col(lwd = 1)+ 
  ylab("Number of studies")+
  facet_wrap(~class, scales = "free_x",
             strip.position = "bottom", nrow = 1)+
  xlab(NULL)+
  scale_fill_manual(name = NULL,
                    values = fill_pal)+
  scale_color_manual(name = "With qualities",
                     values = c("no" = "transparent",
                                "yes" = "gold"))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_blank())

p.sys







Fig. 1. The number of studies found with quantitative evidence on the relationship between cats and threatened species Fill color indicates the article type and whether their results (according to the author’s interpretation) found a negative association between cats and threatened species.
The best evidence per species
Let’s now look at the best evidence available per species that cats are associated with threatened prey declines. To do this, we rank evidence types and select the highest quality type per claimant and species. To do this we also need all claims, e.g., a dataset based on whether a source claimed that cats were a cause of endangerment of a species. We’ll merge the evidence found into this dataset.

Codeclaims <- fread("builds/claims/species_claims_tidy_populated.csv")

# Filter to only included species:
claims <- claims[exclude_species == "included_species", .(spp_name_corrected, scientificName, 
                                                          realm, systems, redlistCategory,
                                                          populationTrend, class)] |> unique()

# Fix the one species that has been split since assessment:
claims[spp_name_corrected == "Prosobonia parvirostris", spp_name_corrected := scientificName]
#

# Copy the systematic review evidence file into a new data structure
ranking <- copy(sys_rev)
ranking <- ranking[, .(spp_name_corrected,
                       of_quality, evidence_type, has_data)]

ranking[of_quality == "yes" &
          evidence_type == "Population in support", rank := 10]
ranking[of_quality == "no" &
          has_data == "yes" &
          evidence_type == "Population in support", rank := 9]
ranking[of_quality == "no" &
          has_data == "no" &
          evidence_type == "Population in support", rank := 8]
ranking[evidence_type == "Predation in support", rank := 7]

ranking[is.na(rank), rank := 0]
ranking[rank == 0, evidence_type := "No evidence in support"]
ranking[rank == 0, has_data := NA]
ranking[rank == 0, of_quality := NA]

ranking <- ranking[, max_rank := max(rank),
                   by = .(spp_name_corrected)]
ranking[, no_evidence := .N, by = .(spp_name_corrected)]
ranking <- ranking[rank == max_rank, ] |> unique()

# Now merge into the claims:
best_evidence <- merge(claims,
                       ranking[, .(spp_name_corrected, evidence_type, of_quality,
                                   has_data)],
                       by = "spp_name_corrected",
                       all.x = T,
                       all.y = T)

#
best_evidence[is.na(redlistCategory), class := "Mammals"]

# 
best_evidence[is.na(evidence_type), evidence_type := "No evidence found"]

best_evidence[is.na(of_quality), of_quality := "no"]
best_evidence[is.na(has_data), has_data := "no"]

best_evidence[grepl("Population", evidence_type), 
              synth_fill := paste(evidence_type, 
                                    ifelse(has_data == "yes", 
                                           "with data", "without data")) |> trimws()]
best_evidence[grepl("Population", evidence_type), 
              synth_fill := paste(synth_fill, 
                                    ifelse(of_quality == "yes",
                                           "and qualities", "")) |> trimws()]
best_evidence[is.na(synth_fill), synth_fill := evidence_type]

fill_pal2 <- c(`Predation in support` = "#a6d3a0", 
               `Population in support without data` = "dodgerblue4", 
               `Population in support with data` = "dodgerblue", 
               `Population in support with data and qualities` = "dodgerblue",
               `No evidence in support` = "grey40",
               `No evidence found` = "black")

best_evidence.freq <- best_evidence[, .(n_species = uniqueN(scientificName)),
                                    by = .(synth_fill,
                                           of_quality, class)]
#

best_evidence.freq$synth_fill <- factor(best_evidence.freq$synth_fill,
                      levels = rev(c("No evidence found", 
                                     "No evidence in support", 
                                     "Predation in support",
                                     "Population in support without data",
                                     "Population in support with data",
                                     "Population in support with data and qualities")))

best_evidence.freq$class <- factor(best_evidence.freq$class,
                                   levels = (c("Birds", "Reptiles", "Mammals",  "Amphibians")))

best.p <- ggplot(data = best_evidence.freq,
       aes(x = class, y = n_species, fill = synth_fill,
           color = of_quality))+
  geom_col(position = position_stack(), width = .75)+
  scale_fill_manual("Best evidence",
                    values = fill_pal2)+
  scale_color_manual("Of quality", 
                     values = c("no" = "transparent",
                                "yes" = "gold"))+
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3),
         color = "none")+
  ylab("Number of species")+
  xlab(NULL)+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.border = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid = element_blank())
best.p



Fig. 2. The best evidence found per species.



The best evidence linking prey species to cats was primarily nothing, followed by records of predation.

title: Introduction
text:
This tutorial walks readers through the analyses associated with:

Wallach, A.D., Pereyra, P., Cuervo, L.M.V., Nakagawa, S., Lundgren, E.J. et al. ‘When consensus procedes the evidence.’ In Submission.

This tutorial assumes a basic understanding of R.
Feel free to clone or download the repo to interact with the code and data directly or to simply follow along in this webpage.
Note that all analyses were conducted in .R scripts in the scripts/ folder of the repo.
Some of the messier data-munging steps (e.g., standardizing text, collapsing or expanding categories) is conducted in these scripts, primarily in the scripts/1_data_mgmt/ directory.
The interactive material on this webpage focuses on the core analyses (mostly in scripts/2_analysis/) and has been copied from these scripts for clearer communication but the original scripts remain in the repo and can be evaluated instead if that is preferred.

sys_rev[, synth_fill := gsub(" in support", ": negative association", synth_fill)]

title: Timeline analysis
text:
Now let’s look at the timeline of the last records of extinct populations attributed to cat predation and the estimated arrival times of cats at those locations. These are reported based on the following categories based on population’s estimated extinction year and estimated cat arrival year:

Extinction before the arrival of cats
Extinction overlaps arrival of cats
Extinction within 0-100 years of cat arrival
Extinction 101-200 years after cat arrival
Extinction >200 years after cat arrival

This workflow corresponds to the full script at scripts/2_analysis/5 timeline analysis.R.
The folded code block below cleans the environment, loads the data, and prepares to plot it. Feel free to click the “Code” button to see the code otherwise, we’ll go straight to calculating the number of species per cat arrival category above:

Coderm(list = ls())

library("readxl")
library("data.table")
library("sf")
library("mapview")
library("rnaturalearth")
library("ggplot2")
library("dplyr")
library("plotly")
library("leafpop")
mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery", "OpenStreetMap", "OpenTopoMap"))

theme_lundy <- theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.border = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.background = element_blank())

# Load data 
data_evidence <- read_xlsx("data/timeline/Cat timeline.xlsx") |> setDT()

#For now exclude one row of Conilurus capricornensis that has NA values
data_evidence <- data_evidence[!is.na(Prey_extirpation_year_earliest), ]

#Exclude Fregilupus varius (the IUCN does not claim that cats caused the extinction of this species)
data_evidence <- data_evidence[scientificName != "Fregilupus varius", ]

#Remove all “uncertain” rows
data_evidence <- data_evidence[is.na(AU_ONLY_Record_certainty) | 
                                 AU_ONLY_Record_certainty == "Confirmed"]

#How many species are in the dataset?

#Change status category to IUCN threat status
iucn_status <- read.csv("data/timeline/iucn_status.csv")
setDT(iucn_status)

full_data <- merge(iucn_status, data_evidence, by.x = "Scientific.name", by.y = "scientificName")

setnames(full_data, "Scientific.name", "Scientific name")
setnames(full_data, "Redlist.category", "Redlist category")

full_data[Class == "AVES", Class :="Birds"]
full_data[Class == "MAMMALIA", Class :="Mammals"]
full_data[Class == "REPTILIA", Class :="Reptiles"]

full_data[, IUCN_status:= NA_character_ ]
full_data[`Redlist category` == "Least Concern", IUCN_status:= "(LC)"]
full_data[`Redlist category` == "Near Threatened", IUCN_status:= "(NT)"]
full_data[`Redlist category` == "Vulnerable", IUCN_status:= "(VU)"]
full_data[`Redlist category` == "Endangered", IUCN_status:= "(EN)"]
full_data[`Redlist category` == "Critically Endangered", IUCN_status:= "(CR)"]
full_data[`Redlist category` == "Extinct in the Wild", IUCN_status:= "(EW)"]
full_data[`Redlist category` == "Extinct", IUCN_status:= "(EX)"]

#Assign color palette for species status
#IUCN palette
IUCN_palette <- list (
  "(LC)" = "#60c759",
  "(NT)" = "#A2CD5A",#"#cde321"
  "(VU)" = "#FFD700", #"#f9e90c",
  "(EN)" = "#fc803d",
  "(CR)" = "#d91801",
  "(EW)" = "#552243",
  "(EX)" = "#000000"
)

full_data <- full_data[, .(Class, Order, Family, Genus, `Scientific name`, `Redlist category`, IUCN_status,
                           Extinction_extirpation, Prey_extirpation_year_earliest, Prey_extirpation_year_earliest_CE_BP,
                           Prey_extirpation_year_latest, Prey_extirpation_year_latest_CE_BP,
                           Prey_extinction_timing_reference, Prey_quote, 
                           Cat_arrival_year_earliest, Cat_arrival_year_earliest_CE_BP, 
                           Cat_arrival_year_latest, Cat_arrival_year_latest_CE_BP, 
                           Cat_arrival_timing_reference, Cat_quote,
                           Location, Country, Latitude, Longitude, Realm, Systems)]

#Remove all LC species
full_data <- full_data[`Redlist category` != "Least Concern",]
full_data[, .N, by=`Redlist category`]
full_data[, .N, by= IUCN_status]

#How many are EX?
spp_list <- unique(full_data[`Redlist category`== "Extinct" | `Redlist category` == "Extinct in the Wild",
                             .(`Scientific name`, `Redlist category`)]) #There are 84 species

#Separate between extinct (EX + EW) and extant threatened species
full_data[, status:= NA_character_]
full_data[, status:= ifelse(`Redlist category`== "Extinct" | `Redlist category`== "Extinct in the Wild", "Extinct", "Extant")]
length(unique(full_data[status=="Extinct", `Scientific name`])) #Okay

# 3. Convert dates from CE to BP--------------------------------------------------
#Earliest prey extirpation → BP (min prey extinction)
full_data[, min_prey_extirpation_year_BP :=
            ifelse(Prey_extirpation_year_earliest_CE_BP == "CE",
                   1950 - Prey_extirpation_year_earliest,
                   Prey_extirpation_year_earliest)
]

#Latest prey extirpation → BP (max prey extinction)
full_data[, max_prey_extirpation_year_BP :=
            ifelse(Prey_extirpation_year_latest_CE_BP == "CE",
                   1950 - Prey_extirpation_year_latest,
                   Prey_extirpation_year_latest)
]

#Earliest cat arrival → BP (min cat arrival)
full_data[, min_cat_arrival_year_BP :=
            ifelse(Cat_arrival_year_earliest_CE_BP == "CE",
                   1950 - Cat_arrival_year_earliest,
                   Cat_arrival_year_earliest)
]

#Latest cat arrival → BP (max cat arrival)
full_data[, max_cat_arrival_year_BP :=
            ifelse(Cat_arrival_year_latest_CE_BP == "CE",
                   1950 - Cat_arrival_year_latest,
                   Cat_arrival_year_latest)
]

#Define time differences (prey extinction − cat arrival)
full_data[, `:=`(
  min_difference = min_prey_extirpation_year_BP - max_cat_arrival_year_BP,
  max_difference = max_prey_extirpation_year_BP - min_cat_arrival_year_BP
)]

full_data[, median_difference := (min_difference + max_difference) / 2]

#Flip direction
full_data[, `:=`(
  min_difference = -min_difference,
  max_difference = -max_difference,
  median_difference = -median_difference
)]

full_data[, prey_window :=
            min_prey_extirpation_year_BP - max_prey_extirpation_year_BP]

full_data[, cat_window :=
            min_cat_arrival_year_BP - max_cat_arrival_year_BP]

full_data[, cat_arrival := NA_character_]

# Before arrival
full_data[min_difference < 0 & max_difference < 0,
          cat_arrival := "Extinction before arrival"]

# Overlaps arrival
full_data[min_difference < 0 & max_difference >= 0,
          cat_arrival := "Extinction overlaps arrival"]

# 0–100 years
full_data[min_difference >= 0 & min_difference <= 100,
          cat_arrival := "Extinction within 100 years of arrival"]

# 101-200 years
full_data[min_difference > 100 & min_difference <= 200,
          cat_arrival := "Extinction 101–200 years after arrival"]

# >200 years
full_data[min_difference > 200,
          cat_arrival := "Extinction 201 years or more after arrival"]

full_data$cat_arrival <- factor(full_data$cat_arrival,
                                levels = c(
                                  "Extinction 201 years or more after arrival",
                                  "Extinction 101–200 years after arrival",
                                  "Extinction within 100 years of arrival",
                                  "Extinction overlaps arrival",
                                  "Extinction before arrival"
                                ))

full_data <- full_data[, .(Class, Order, Family, Genus, `Scientific name`, status, Extinction_extirpation,
                           `Redlist category`, IUCN_status, Location, Country, Latitude, Longitude, Realm, Systems,
                           Prey_extirpation_year_earliest, Prey_extirpation_year_earliest_CE_BP,
                           Prey_extirpation_year_latest, Prey_extirpation_year_latest_CE_BP,
                           Prey_extinction_timing_reference, Prey_quote, 
                           Cat_arrival_year_earliest, Cat_arrival_year_earliest_CE_BP,

text:
Prey body mass
Does body mass modulate the association between cats and prey? As we showed here, body mass was primarily derived from Phylacine (for mammals) and AvoNet (for birds).

                      only_dominant_effect_size == "no" &

# Prepare for app ----------------------------------------------------------
labels <- c(`Core claim` = "Core claim", 
            `External review without claim` = "External source without claim", 
            `Nothing cited` = "Nothing cited",
            `Excluded` = "No primary data found", 
            `Predation in support without data` = "Predation record without data", 
            `Predation not in support without data` = "Predation record without data", 
            `Population in support without data` = "Population - description", 
            `Population in support with data` = "Population - study",
            `Population not in support without data` = "Population - description", 
            `Population not in support with data` = "Population - study")

node_fill <- c(`Core claim` = "hotpink", `External review without claim` = "pink", 
               Excluded = "grey", `Nothing cited` = "black", 
               `Predation in support without data` = "#a6d3a0", 
               `Predation not in support without data` = "#40531b", 
               `Population not in support without data` = "indianred4", `Population not in support with data` = "indianred", 
               `Population in support without data` = "dodgerblue4", `Population in support with data` = "dodgerblue"
)
node_size <- c(`Core claim` = 5, `External review without claim` = 5, `Opportunistic` = 1,
               Excluded = 1, 
               `Predation without data` = 2, #`Control program without data` = 2, 
               `Population without data` = 3, `Population with data` = 4)

stroke_color <- c("no" = "black", 
                  "yes" = "gold")

stroke_width <- c("no" = .01, 
                  "yes" = 2)

# Shiny app ----------------------------------------------------------------------
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel(""),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput(
        inputId = "spp",
        label = "Select a species",
        choices = sort(unique(edges$scientificName)),
        selected = sort(unique(edges$scientificName))[1]
      ),
      htmlOutput(outputId = "references")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput(outputId = "citationPlot")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$citationPlot <- renderPlot({
    edges.sub <- edges[scientificName %in% input$spp, ]
    nodes.sub <- nodes[node_id %in% unique(c(edges.sub$cited_by_id,
                                              edges.sub$article_id)), ]
    nodes.sub[, node_label := as.numeric(as.factor(node_id))]
    igraph.gr <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(d = edges.sub, 
                                           vertices = nodes.sub,
                                           directed = T)
    igraph.gr

    graph <- tidygraph::as_tbl_graph(igraph.gr)
    
    ggraph(graph, layout = "kk")+
        geom_edge_fan(arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, 'mm')), 
                      start_cap = circle(2, 'mm'),
                      end_cap = circle(2, 'mm'),
                      color = "black",
                      # alpha = .5,
                      linewidth = 0.5) + 
        geom_node_point(aes(fill = evidence_type_synthetic_simple,
                            color = of_quality,
                            stroke = of_quality,
                            size = evidence_type_simple), 
                        shape = 21, 
                        alpha = .75)+
        geom_node_label(aes(label = node_label),
                        nudge_y = 0.1,
                        vjust = 0)+
        scale_fill_manual("Article type",
                          values = node_fill,
                          labels = labels)+
        scale_size_manual("Article type",
                          values = node_size *2,
                          breaks = levels(nodes$evidence_type_simple))+ 
        guides(size = "none",
               fill = "none",
               color = "none",
               stroke = "none")+
        scale_discrete_manual("Quality research",
                              aesthetics = "stroke", 
                              values = c(1, 2))+
        scale_color_manual("Quality research",
                           values = stroke_color )+
        theme_graph()+
        theme(legend.position = 'bottom')
  })
  
  output$references <- renderUI({
    edges.sub <- edges[scientificName %in% input$spp, ]
    nodes.sub <- nodes[node_id %in% unique(c(edges.sub$cited_by_id,
                                              edges.sub$article_id)), ]
    nodes.sub[, node_label := as.numeric(as.factor(node_id))]
    nodes.sub[, node_name_clean := ifelse(grepl("NOTHING", article_node_name),
                                          "Nothing cited", 
                                          article_node_name)]
    nodes.sub[, node_name_clean := gsub("(", "", node_name_clean, fixed = TRUE)]
    nodes.sub[, node_name_clean := gsub(")", "", node_name_clean, fixed = TRUE)]

    nodes.sub[, node_description := paste0(node_label, ": ", node_name_clean)]
    
    HTML(paste("References:<br>",
          paste(nodes.sub$node_description, collapse = "<br>")))
  })
}
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
